requirements: Explain how the war enabled Polish independence; evaluate political, military and international mechanisms

aspects.name: political

facts.claim: In November 1918 the Regency Council transferred military then civil authority to Piłsudski.
The Polish Liquidation Commission was formed in Kraków on 28 October 1918 to take authority over former Austrian-partition lands.

aspects.causal_explanation: Wartime imperial breakdown opened space for Polish authorities. The Kraków commission and transfer of existing administrative authority helped consolidate the emerging state; Polish institutions used the opening rather than receiving complete borders automatically.

aspects.name: military

facts.claim: Polish Legions were organized with Austrian approval in 1914; Piłsudski and Legion soldiers broke with the German oath in 1917.

aspects.causal_explanation: Military organization supplied cadres while the oath crisis demonstrates that alignment with a partitioning power was tactical.

aspects.name: international

facts.claim: Wilson publicly called for an independent Poland with access to the sea in point XIII.
Germany signed the western-front armistice at Compiègne on 11 November 1918.

aspects.causal_explanation: International endorsement made restoration a stated war aim, while German military defeat removed a major occupying constraint. Neither declaration nor armistice alone settled all Polish borders.

traps.claim_or_issue: Independence and all borders were settled by Wilson or on 11 November 1918.
traps.correction_or_caveat: The speech is a proposal;11 November transferred military authority,14 November civil authority. Do not equate those acts with a completed territorial settlement.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Accept different weights for military organization, diplomacy and partitioning-power collapse if evidence connects them.

requirements: Compare Piłsudski and Dmowski: initial alignments, instruments and evolution during the war

aspects.name: Piłsudski: armed initiative and tactical alignment

facts.claim: Legion formation accompanied Austrian cooperation; Piłsudski was imprisoned after the 1917 oath refusal.

aspects.causal_explanation: Armed cadres were intended as leverage; breaking the oath prevents describing his position as permanent German loyalty.

aspects.name: Dmowski: Entente diplomacy

facts.claim: Dmowski headed the 1917 Polish National Committee, recognized by France and other Entente powers.

aspects.causal_explanation: Diplomatic recognition furnished an external representation for Polish claims, distinct from Piłsudski’s domestic military route.

traps.correction_or_caveat: An exclusive assertion needs evidence accounting for the other route and international conditions; disagreement about relative importance is interpretive.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: These comparison dimensions organize evaluation; they are not extra aspects imposed by an official marking key.

requirements: Explain defeat in September 1939 using international and military aspects

aspects.name: international

facts.claim: Britain and France declared war on 3 September; the Soviet invasion followed on 17 September.

aspects.causal_explanation: A declaration did not supply a timely relieving offensive; invasion from the east compounded German pressure.

aspects.name: military

facts.claim: Germany held major military superiority and combined aircraft and armored movement; Poland subsequently faced two invading powers.

aspects.causal_explanation: Material and operational asymmetry plus a second front explain defeat more concretely than a claim of Polish cowardice.

traps.claim_or_issue: Poland surrendered nationally on 17 September or cavalry routinely charged tanks.
traps.correction_or_caveat: The last operational Polish unit surrendered 6 October. The cavalry claim is not established by these sources and requires checking rather than repeating.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Permit arguments weighing operational plans, mobilization or geography when separately supported; no single-cause thesis is required.

requirements: Distinguish public nonaggression from the secret protocol; explain regional consequences

aspects.name: agreement and spheres

facts.claim: The public treaty signed on 23 August 1939 pledged mutual nonaggression, non-support for a third power attacking either signatory, and exclusion from hostile groupings.
facts.locator: Articles I, II and IV; signature date

facts.claim: The secret protocol of 23 August 1939 assigned spheres in Eastern Europe; its Polish clause used the Narew–Vistula–San line.
The secret protocol placed Finland, Estonia and Latvia in the Soviet sphere and recorded Soviet interest in Bessarabia; the initial Baltic dividing line was Lithuania’s northern boundary.

aspects.causal_explanation: Public promises removed the immediate prospect of war between the signatories, while secret territorial understandings reduced the diplomatic obstacle to aggression. Distinguish the August spheres from later border revisions and actual occupations.

aspects.name: consequences

facts.claim: Germany invaded 1 September, the USSR 17 September; the defeated country was partitioned.
facts.locator: Key Facts; Invasion and Partition of Poland

aspects.causal_explanation: The military implementation turned diplomatic spheres into occupation, while later border arrangements must be dated separately.

traps.claim_or_issue: The August protocol used exactly the final September occupation border.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Read the August river line as written; distinguish the subsequent partition from the original clause.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: A regional analysis may also discuss Baltic or Bessarabian clauses; do not demand exact full-document recitation.

requirements: Evaluate political, military and cultural effects of Alexander’s conquests

aspects.name: political

facts.claim: Successor dynasties included Ptolemies in Egypt, Seleucids in the Near East and Antigonids in Macedonia.

aspects.causal_explanation: Conquest enabled new monarchies; their continuation need not imply survival of one unified empire.

aspects.name: military

facts.claim: Alexander’s campaigns from 334 to 323 BCE extended through Egypt and the Persian realm toward India.

aspects.causal_explanation: Campaign reach displaced the prior imperial order and exposed the limits of maintaining control across a huge territory.

aspects.name: cultural

facts.claim: Conquest and subsequent mobility widened exchange between Greek and other traditions.
The Hellenistic successor world developed great libraries at Alexandria and Pergamon.
facts.locator: Paragraph beginning Hellenistic art is richly diverse

aspects.causal_explanation: Conquest widened contact; successor patronage supported scholarly and artistic centers, illustrated by these libraries. This is a consequence of the Hellenistic world, not a claim that Alexander personally founded every institution or replaced all local cultures.

traps.claim_or_issue: Alexander created one culturally uniform empire lasting intact for centuries.
traps.correction_or_caveat: The source distinguishes a short-lived united empire from varied successor kingdoms and cultures.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Credit both creative exchange and violent imperial domination when the essay supplies sound evidence.

requirements: Explain disintegration after Alexander’s death rather than merely list successor states

aspects.name: loss of central authority and successor competition

facts.claim: Alexander died in 323 BCE; his generals divided the lands into their own kingdoms.

aspects.causal_explanation: Inference: an empire assembled around military leadership was vulnerable when commanders established territorial power after that leader’s death. Treat the inference as an argument, not a quoted source claim.

traps.claim_or_issue: All mature successor kingdoms appeared instantly and without conflict in 323 BCE.
traps.correction_or_caveat: The museum gives the general succession process; it does not justify exact instantaneous state borders or every succession-war date.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Other causal accounts involving succession arrangements or regional resistance are valid if independently sourced; no dynastic event list is compulsory.

requirements: Explain causes and consequences of 1956 in Poland: political, social and economic

aspects.name: political

facts.claim: Khrushchev criticized Stalin in February 1956; October brought Gomułka’s return amid Soviet pressure.

aspects.causal_explanation: Destalinization weakened established authority and opened conflict over change, without proving the end of communist government.

aspects.name: social

facts.claim: Poznań workers demonstrated 28 June; the authorities sent regular army units and suppressed the revolt.
October also brought widespread demonstrations and attempts at independent organization.

aspects.causal_explanation: Repression deepened the legitimacy crisis; later mobilization shows social consequences.

aspects.name: economic

facts.claim: Falling real wages, shortages and production pressures contributed to protest.
After October, peasants dissolved collective farms.
facts.locator: Final paragraph on rural responses to October

aspects.causal_explanation: Material grievances drove protest; rural dissolution illustrates an economic consequence of the political opening.

traps.claim_or_issue: 1956 ended PZPR rule or Soviet influence.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Gomułka’s October appeal still defended relations with the USSR; distinguish partial change from systemic independence.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Credit accounts emphasizing social pressure, internal party struggle or international context if they connect causes and outcomes.

requirements: Explain the June protest’s course and significance

aspects.name: course

facts.claim: Workers came onto Poznań streets 28 June over pay, norms and shortages; repression involved regular troops.

aspects.causal_explanation: Failed handling of demands and repression escalated a labor dispute into a challenge to communist power.

aspects.name: significance

facts.claim: The Poznań revolt catalyzed subsequent debate and social mobilization in 1956.

aspects.causal_explanation: Its significance lies in pressure on the regime, not an immediate successful seizure of national power.

traps.claim_or_issue: Gomułka was already party leader during the June revolt; June and October were the same event.
traps.correction_or_caveat: Keep June repression distinct from the October leadership transition. Exact casualty totals vary across historical compilations; do not penalize a plausible sourced count automatically.

topics.interpretive_flexibility: Revolt, uprising and workers’ protest may be defensible labels; evaluate explained content rather than enforce one label.
